cards.explanation: The answer is kindness, friends. David, Israel's king, says, “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me.” Hanun is the new king of the Ammonites, and David wants to answer kindness with kindness.

The answer is True, friends. The text says David sent some of his servants to console Hanun concerning his father. That's a sympathy visit, the kind where you show up and say, "I'm so sorry for your loss." David meant it as comfort, and that's the whole plan.

The answer is that they say the servants are there to spy out the city and overthrow it. The princes ask Hanun, “Has not David instead sent his servants to explore the city, spy it out, and overthrow it?” Notice they ask it as a question, with David's kind visit sitting right there, friends. They're saying the comforters are scouts.

The answer is half, friends. The text says Hanun shaved off half of each man's beard. I think this one hurts, so I'll say it plainly. David's servants came to comfort and were treated this way instead.

The answer is after their beards grow back, friends. David tells them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return.” Before that, he sends messengers to meet them. That's a king looking after his men. And a beard has its own timer, one that nobody can speed up.

The answer is False, friends. When the Ammonites realized they had become a stench to David, they hired soldiers. They didn't send a gift. Their answer to becoming a stench to David was to bring in an army, and that's all the text tells us.

The answer is that David sends out the entire army of mighty men, friends. The text says, “…David sent Joab and the entire army of mighty men.” Joab is David's commander (2 Samuel 8:16). The Ammonites hired a crowd, and David answered with his whole army of mighty men.

The answer is that Joab splits the army into two groups, friends. He picks some of Israel's best men to face the Arameans, then puts the rest under his brother Abishai to face the Ammonites. One army, two fronts. Joab saw the battle lines before him and behind him and set up his troops.

The answer is best, friends. The text says Joab “…selected some of the best men of Israel…” and lined them up against the Arameans (2 Samuel 10:9). He saw battle lines before him and behind him, so he picked his strongest for the Arameans. Abishai gets the rest of the troops, who face the Ammonites.

The plan is that if one of them is overpowered, the other comes to help, friends. Joab tells Abishai, “then you will come to my rescue. And if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come to your rescue.” It's like two friends texting, "Just yell if you need me." Each brother is covering the other.

The answer is True, friends. Joab says, “Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God.” He says it right after telling Abishai how they'll rescue each other. That's a pep talk with real stakes behind it.
The answer is False, friends. Joab and his troops advance to fight the Arameans, and the Arameans fled before him. That's quick. Then the Ammonites see it and run too (2 Samuel 10:14).

The answer is Shobach, friends. He's the commander of Hadadezer's army, and he leads the new Aramean troops to Helam. Hadadezer, king of Zobah (2 Samuel 8:3), is the one who sent for them. Keep that name, because Shobach's story ends there.

The answer is False, friends. When the report reaches David, “…he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and went to Helam.” He doesn't stay in Jerusalem. The Arameans then line up against David himself.

The answer is that they flee before Israel, friends. The text says the Arameans “…fled before Israel…” The text even tells us David killed seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers, and struck down Shobach. It's a heavy part, so I'll leave it at that.

The answer is that they make peace and become subject to Israel, friends. The text says that when all the kings subject to Hadadezer saw they had been defeated by Israel, they “…made peace with Israel and became subject to them.” Those are the kings who had stood behind Hadadezer. They end up making peace with Israel.
The answer is False, friends. The text says, “So the Arameans were afraid to help the Ammonites anymore.” Afraid is the word the text uses. The kings had made peace with Israel by then.
